title: Consider a builder when faced with many constructor parameters
concept: Telescoping constructors (parameter bloat) become hard to read, write, and maintain when a class has many optional parameters. The JavaBeans pattern (getters/setters) allows construction, but leaves objects in an inconsistent, mutable state mid-construction. The Builder pattern combines the safety of telescoping constructors with the readability of JavaBeans, allowing immutable instances with fluent, readable construction.

when_to_use_flashcard.front: When should you prefer the Builder pattern over constructors or static factories?
when_to_use_flashcard.back: When designing classes with more than a few parameters, especially if many are optional or share the same primitive type (e.g. multiple ints or Strings).

when_not_to_use_flashcard.front: When is a Builder unnecessary overhead?
when_not_to_use_flashcard.back: When a class has only 2–3 required fields with few or no optional parameters. A simple constructor or static factory is much cleaner and avoids extra builder allocation.

quiz.question: What is the primary danger of the JavaBeans pattern (using default constructor followed by setters)?
options: It prevents objects from using primitive types
It leaves the object in an inconsistent state midway through construction and precludes immutability
It cannot be used with JSON serialization
It requires significantly more memory than a builder

quiz.question: How does the Builder pattern ensure the constructed object is immutable?
options: By enforcing final fields on the target class and passing builder state through a private constructor
By running inside a synchronized block
By preventing garbage collection
By restricting all methods to static methods

quiz.question: Where should parameter invariant validation take place when using the Builder pattern?
options: Only in client code before calling the builder
Inside the target class's constructor or build() method on the copied fields
Only inside getter methods
Validation is not possible when using the Builder pattern

quiz.question: What design technique allows builders to work smoothly across class hierarchies (subclasses)?
options: Abstract classes with recursive type parameters (simulated self-types)
Overloading static factories
Reflection
Multiple inheritance of classes

quiz.question: Why is the telescoping constructor pattern error-prone even if code compiles without warnings?
options: Callers can easily swap arguments of the same type without the compiler complaining
Constructors cannot call other constructors using this()
It cannot exceed 3 parameters on modern JVMs
Java limits classes to at most two constructors

interview_questions.question: Compare the Builder pattern with Telescoping Constructors and JavaBeans. What tradeoffs does Builder make?
interview_questions.model_answer: Telescoping constructors are safe and immutable but scale terribly with many parameters. JavaBeans are readable but allow inconsistent states and mutable objects. Builder provides the best of both: readable fluent syntax while preserving strict immutability and thread safety, at the cost of a small initial builder allocation.

interview_questions.question: A developer validates builder invariants inside the setter methods `builder.foo(val)` instead of in `build()`. What is the flaw?
interview_questions.model_answer: Validating inside setters fails to catch invalid combinations across multiple fields that might depend on one another. Cross-field invariants must be validated in `build()` or the class constructor once all parameters are supplied.

interview_questions.question: Can you use the Builder pattern with class hierarchies (such as abstract Pizza and concrete NyPizza / Calzone)? How?
interview_questions.model_answer: Yes, by using an abstract builder with a recursive type parameter (simulated self-type, e.g. `Builder<T extends Builder<T>>`). Concrete subclasses return `this` cast to `T`, allowing fluent method chaining across subclass hierarchies without explicit downcasts.

interview_questions.question: How do libraries like Project Lombok's `@Builder` implement this pattern, and what is one caveat to keep in mind?
interview_questions.model_answer: Lombok generates the static inner Builder class, fluent setters, and private constructor at compile time via annotation processing. A key caveat is ensuring default field values and validation checks are properly configured, as simple `@Builder` without `@Builder.Default` can ignore inline field initializers.
